title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
The bus stop

Agnes, Beatrice, Clara, Dorothy and Batman waiting at a bus stopIllustration generated with Gemini, prompted by Doug Manuel. Batman is the property of DC Comics.

Who will get on the first bus? Who will let whom on?
Batman is the polite superhero. Everyone in the class has just made a prediction.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
From picture to data


riders <- data.frame(
  rider     = c("Agnes", "Beatrice", "Clara", "Dorothy", "Batman"),
  age       = c(35, 80, 85, 80, 40),
  cane      = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0),
  superhero = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1),
  boarded   = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0), # got on the first bus
  minutes   = c(35, 15.5, 15, 15.25, 35.25) # after 8:00
)


The first bus has room for three. Observed: 3 of 5 boarded, or 0.60.
age, cane, superhero: the predictors (in machine learning, features). boarded: the outcome (label or target).

This is our database. Every later calculation uses these column names: riders\(age, riders\)boarded, and the model columns on the next slide. Beatrice and Dorothy are the same age.
The order they got on: Clara first (she has the cane and the others let her on), then Dorothy, then Beatrice. The first bus is full. Agnes, the youngest, and Batman, the polite superhero, wait for the next bus. We use the minutes later.

Which model is better?


Model A knows the cane helps and that superheroes wait, but its intercept is too high: it thinks everyone is likely to board. Model B ignores the cane and thinks superheroes push to the front. Beatrice and Dorothy are the same age, so each model gives them the same probability: a tie.
Ask the class to vote before going on.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Discrimination
Who gets on the bus first?

How well the predictions differentiate between individuals with and without the outcome.


Calibration
When do they get on the bus?

Agreement between observed outcomes and estimated values from the model.



TRIPOD+AI. BMJ 2024;385. doi:10.1136/bmj-2023-078378


Discrimination is about ranking: does the model put people in the right order? Calibration is about whether the predicted values match what is observed. Discrimination is usually quantified by the c statistic (also called AUC or AUROC for binary outcomes). Today we put numbers on both, using the bus stop.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
The c statistic counts pairs
Pair each rider who boarded with each rider who did not: 3 × 2 = 6 pairs. The c statistic is also called the concordance statistic, and in machine learning the AUC.
A pair is concordant when the model gives the rider who boarded the higher probability.
\[
c = \frac{\text{concordant pairs} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\text{tied pairs}}{\text{all pairs}}
\]

\(c = 1\): perfect ranking
\(c = 0.5\): no better than a coin toss


For a binary outcome the c statistic equals the area under the ROC curve. Counting pairs is the same quantity, and it is easier to see what it means. We come back to the ROC in a few slides.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Model A ranks perfectly; Model B is a coin toss
text:
Model A ranks perfectly; Model B is a coin toss

Green arrow: who got on. Black arrow: the model’s pick (higher probability). Arrows point at the rider: ↑ column, ← row. Grey: both got on, or both waited, so not compared.

Read one cell first: Agnes and Beatrice. Beatrice got on, so the green arrow points up at her. Model A gives Beatrice 0.90 and Agnes 0.85, so its black arrow also points up: they agree, the cell is green. Count the green cells and divide by the cells that are not grey: that is c. Model B’s whole Batman column is red: it is sure Batman will board, and he waits.

title: Calibration and discrimination
Calibration and discrimination
text:
The same count in R

p <- riders$model_b # try model_a too
pairs <- expand.grid(
  boarded = which(riders$boarded == 1),
  waited = which(riders$boarded == 0)
)
better <- p[pairs$boarded] > p[pairs$waited]
tied <- p[pairs$boarded] == p[pairs$waited]
mean(better + 0.5 * tied)

[1] 0.5



Line by line: choose the model, build every boarded and not-boarded pairing, flag the pairs ranked correctly and the ties, then average with ties counting half. This is the same number as the hand calculation.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: From pairs to a curve: the ROC
text:
From pairs to a curve: the ROC
Pick a threshold \(t\) and predict “boards” for anyone with \(p \ge t\). Every threshold gives a different yes/no prediction:
\[
\text{sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{\text{boarded } (3)}
\qquad
1 - \text{specificity} = \frac{FP}{\text{waited } (2)}
\]
Model B. \(TP\), true positives: predicted to board, and did. \(FP\), false positives: predicted to board, but waited. Machine learning calls sensitivity recall or the true positive rate, and 1 − specificity the false positive rate.

section: ROC curves for Models A and B
text:
ROC curves for Models A and B

The dashed diagonal is a coin toss.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: The area under the curve is the c statistic
text:
The area under the curve is the c statistic
Add up the trapezoids: each step adds width × average height, \(\Delta x \times \tfrac{1}{2}(\text{sens}_{k-1} + \text{sens}_k)\).
\(\Delta x\): the step in 1 − specificity. \(\text{sens}_k\): sensitivity at threshold \(k\).
\[
\text{area}_B = 0.00 + 0.00 + 0.00 + 0.50 = {\color{#b03030}\mathbf{0.50}}
\]
The same number as counting pairs: \(c_B\) = 0.50.

# rb: the ROC table from two slides back
rb <- roc_points(riders$model_b, riders$boarded)
dx <- diff(rb$fpr)
height <- (head(rb$tpr, -1) + tail(rb$tpr, -1)) / 2
sum(dx * height)

[1] 0.5



Two routes to the same quantity: count the correctly ranked pairs, or integrate the ROC curve. For a binary outcome they are identical, and ties get half credit either way.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: A word of caution about the ROC
text:
A word of caution about the ROC

The ROC curve is everywhere in machine learning. In medicine it is debated.
It summarises ranking over every threshold, including thresholds nobody would use.
It ignores calibration. Model A has c = 1.00 but predicts 0.86 on average when 0.60 boarded.
It ignores the costs of false positives and false negatives at the threshold you actually choose.
Report it alongside a calibration plot, and a decision-focused measure such as net benefit (the good done by true positives minus the harm of false positives, at the threshold you use).


Keep this short. The point is that a high c alone does not make a model useful, which is why the next section is about calibration.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Calibration-in-the-large: compare the averages
\[
O = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i \qquad E = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} p_i
\]
O, observed: the share who boarded. E, expected: the average predicted probability. \(N\) = 5 riders. \(y_i\): rider \(i\)’s boarded (1 = got on, 0 = waited). \(p_i\): rider \(i\)’s predicted probability (model_a or model_b).
\[
O = \frac{0 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0}{5} = 0.60
\]
\[
E_A = \frac{0.85 + 0.90 + 0.96 + 0.90 + 0.69}{5} = \frac{4.30}{5} = 0.86
\]
\[
E_B = \frac{0.44 + 0.55 + 0.56 + 0.55 + 0.91}{5} = \frac{3.01}{5} = 0.60
\]

Calibration-in-the-large only checks the average. Model B matches on average, yet its predictions for individual riders are poor. Seeing calibration across the range of risk needs a calibration plot, and that needs more than five riders.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Observed against predicted
\[
\text{O/E}_A = \frac{0.60}{0.86} = 0.70
\qquad
\text{O/E}_B = \frac{0.60}{0.60} = 1.00
\]

Model A over-predicts by 43%: “much higher” (more than 20%) on the scale used to judge the Framingham equations in Canada.

Grey is what happened: 3 of 5 boarded. Blue is what each model expected on average. Model A’s bar is too tall: it over-predicts. Model B’s bars match, even though its ranking is poor. Calibration-in-the-large only checks the average.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Brier score: average squared error
\[
\text{Brier} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} (p_i - y_i)^2
\]
\(p_i\): predicted probability (model_a, model_b). \(y_i\): boarded, 1 or 0. \(N\) = 5 riders. In machine learning, the Brier score is the mean squared error of the probabilities.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Picturing the Brier score

Blue: the prediction. White: what happened (1 = boarded, 0 = waited). The red line is the error; the number under each rider is its square. Average the squares.

Each red line is one rider’s error. Squaring makes the long lines count much more: Model B’s line for Batman alone is 0.83, more than any of Model A’s. Model A’s lines are short for the riders who boarded and long for Agnes and Batman, because it thinks everyone boards.

section: The Brier score mixes both problems
text:
The Brier score mixes both problems


Model A
Perfect ranking (c = 1.00), yet a Brier score of 0.24, no better than predicting 0.60 for everyone

Model B
Right on average (O/E = 1.00), yet a Brier score of 0.32, worse still


One number cannot tell you which problem a model has. Report discrimination and calibration separately (TRIPOD+AI).

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: F1 and accuracy mix them too
text:
F1 and accuracy mix them too
Machine learning often scores a model at a threshold: predict “boards” if \(p \ge 0.50\).






Model A
Model B




Precision (PPV) = TP / (TP + FP)
3 / 5 = 0.60
3 / 4 = 0.75


Recall (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN)
3 / 3 = 1.00

F1 \(= \dfrac{2 \times \text{precision} \times \text{recall}}{\text{precision} + \text{recall}}\). Precision is the positive predictive value (PPV): the share of predicted boarders who boarded. Recall is sensitivity. TN, true negatives: predicted to wait, and did.

By F1, the coin-toss model wins.


Model A puts everyone above 0.5, so it predicts that all five board: precision 0.60, recall 1.00. Model B predicts everyone but Agnes boards, including Batman. F1 depends on the ranking, on where the predictions sit relative to the threshold (calibration), on the threshold itself and on how common the outcome is, and it ignores true negatives. So a single F1 cannot tell you which problem a model has. After recalibration, Model A’s F1 at 0.5 becomes 0.86 with c unchanged at 1.00. In health and medicine, report discrimination and calibration separately, and judge thresholds by their clinical consequences (net benefit).

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Recalibrate Model A: shift the log-odds
text:
Recalibrate Model A: shift the log-odds
\[
\text{logit}(p_i^{*}) = \text{logit}(p_i) + a
\]
Estimate \(a\) with a logistic regression that has \(\text{logit}(p_i)\) as an offset: \(a\) = −1.58
\(p_i^{*}\): rider \(i\)’s recalibrated probability. \(a\): one shift, the same for every rider. An offset keeps \(\text{logit}(p_i)\) fixed, so only \(a\) is estimated.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Recalibration cannot fix discrimination

Same constant added to every log-odds: same order, same arrows. Model A can be repaired; Model B needs new coefficients, a new model.

The probabilities change (0.86 on average becomes 0.60), but no black arrow moves. Recalibration cannot turn a red cell green. In the formula, recalibration only changes Model A’s intercept, from 2.0 to 0.42.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Boarding times

Everyone reaches the stop at 8:00. Order of boarding: Clara, Dorothy, Beatrice, Agnes, Batman.

These times are made up. Clara gets on first, Dorothy 15 seconds later, then Beatrice. The bus is full, so Agnes and Batman take the second bus. Most medical prediction models are like this: the outcome is the time to an event.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
A model for time
\[
h_i(t) = h_0(t)\,\exp(\text{lp}_i)
\]
\[
\text{lp}_i = 0.1\,\tfrac{\text{age} - 60}{10} + 1.0\,\text{cane} - 1.0\,\text{superhero}
\]
\[
S_i(t) = S_0(t)^{\exp(\text{lp}_i)} \qquad P_i(\text{on a bus by } t) = 1 - S_i(t)
\]
\(\text{lp}_i\): the linear predictor, the weighted sum of rider \(i\)’s predictors (Model A’s slopes, no intercept). \(h_i(t)\): rider \(i\)’s hazard, the chance of boarding in the next moment if still waiting. \(h_0(t)\): the baseline hazard. \(\exp(\text{lp}_i)\): the hazard ratio. \(S_i(t)\): the chance rider \(i\) is still waiting at time \(t\). \(S_0(t)\): the baseline survival, the chance a rider with \(\text{lp} = 0\) is still waiting at \(t\).

The same slopes as Model A, but no intercept: the baseline takes its place.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Predictions for 8:20
\(S_0(\text{8:20}) = 0.41\), set so the average prediction matches the on-time day, so \(P_i(\text{on a bus by 8:20}) = 1 - 0.41^{\exp(\text{lp}_i)}\).

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: With time: who got on first?
text:
With time: who got on first?

Green arrow: who got on first. Black arrow: the model’s pick. Everyone boarded at a different time, so no cell is grey.

Same grid as before, now with time. The grey cells are filled in: Clara against Dorothy, Agnes against Batman, and so on. Model A agrees everywhere except Beatrice against Dorothy: same age, same probability, so that pair scores half. This is why we only score pairs with different outcomes: with the yes-or-no outcome Beatrice and Dorothy both boarded, so their tie never counted. Model B gets every pair with Batman wrong, and ties Beatrice and Dorothy too.

title: Calibration and discrimination
Calibration and discrimination
section: The same count in R, with time
text:
The same count in R, with time

library(survival)
riders$event <- 1 # everyone boards eventually
fit <- concordance(
  Surv(minutes, event) ~ model_b,
  data = riders,
  reverse = TRUE # higher p = earlier boarding
)
fit$concordance

[1] 0.55



Surv() pairs each time with whether the event happened. reverse = TRUE tells R that a higher predicted probability should go with a shorter time. The answer matches the hand count.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Rank order: the same pairs, without the clock
text:
Rank order: the same pairs, without the clock

Left: the order they got on. Right: the order the model predicted. Each crossing is a pair the model got backwards; lines that meet are a tie.

Ranks only, no clock. Model A’s lines never cross; Beatrice and Dorothy meet because the model gives them the same probability. Model B’s Batman line crosses all four others: the model puts him first, and he got on last.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Somers’ D: right minus wrong
\[
D = \frac{\text{concordant} - \text{discordant}}{\text{all pairs}} = 2c - 1
\]
\[
D_A = \frac{9 - 0}{10} = 0.90
\qquad
D_B = \frac{5 - 4}{10} = 0.10
\]

Ties count in “all pairs” but neither add nor subtract. In machine learning, 2 × AUC − 1 is called the Gini coefficient: the same quantity. A ranking has no probabilities, so there is nothing to calibrate.

c and Somers’ D carry the same information on different scales. c runs from 0.5 (coin toss) to 1 (perfect); Somers’ D runs from 0 to 1, and down to −1 for a model that ranks everyone exactly backwards. Model A: 9 right, 0 wrong, 1 tie. Model B: 5 right, 4 wrong (all the pairs with Batman), 1 tie. Rank-order outcomes are common in machine learning (search, recommendation) and often neglected in medicine.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
The bus is 15 minutes late

Same riders, same order. Every boarding is 15 minutes later.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Same ranking, broken calibration
The Cox model’s predictions for 8:20 do not change: same riders, same order.


Discrimination is about order, so a late bus cannot change it. Calibration is about the time to event.


The same picture as observed against predicted for Models A and B. The blue bars are identical: the model sees the same riders. On the late day nobody is on a bus by 8:20, so the grey bar is empty and O/E falls to zero. The order of boarding is unchanged, so c is the same on both days.
This is the example from the lecture: near-perfect discrimination, and the bus comes late, so calibration is terrible. In medicine the late bus is a change in baseline risk: a new population, better treatment, a different era. Predictions are made for a horizon, such as the 5-year risk of stroke.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
The baseline is the timetable

Before a bus comes nobody can board, so \(S_0(t) = 1\); each bus is a step down. A model that takes \(S_0\) from the published timetable is calibrated only when the buses run on time.

The heights between buses are illustrative, anchored at the 0.41 we set for 8:20. The dotted line is 8:20: on time, a rider with lp = 0 has a 0.41 chance of still waiting; when the buses are late, 1.00.
There are two ways to get a baseline. Usually it is estimated from the data: the observed boarding times (in a Cox model, the Breslow estimator). Or it comes from a published source: here the bus timetable; in medicine, a life table or a registry for baseline mortality or incidence. Either way, the predictors set the order and the baseline sets the clock. Using a model somewhere new is like trusting another city’s timetable. If the day is known to matter (snow, rush hour), a model can carry one baseline per kind of day: a stratified Cox model.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Calibration depends on the time horizon
text:
Calibration depends on the time horizon





Observed
On time
15 minutes late

1.00

The late bus changes the baseline, \(S_0(t)\). On the late day nobody is on a bus by 8:20, so \(S_0(\text{8:20})\) should be 1.00, not 0.41.
The linear predictor \(\text{lp}_i\), which sets the order, is untouched. Recalibrating means re-estimating \(S_0(t)\) for the new day, just as we shifted the intercept for Model A.

The late day at 8:40 looks like the on-time day at 8:20. Calibration has to be checked at the horizon the model is used for. \(S_i(t)\) is rider i’s chance of still waiting at time t.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Why calibration is harder than discrimination
text:
Why calibration is harder than discrimination

Age, cane and superhero status tell us who gets on before whom: the order
Nothing in our data says when the bus comes. That is the baseline, \(S_0(t)\): the timetable, the traffic, the day
Discrimination needs only the order, so it travels from one bus stop to another
Calibration needs the order and the baseline, so it has to be checked, and often re-estimated, wherever the model is used


In medicine the baseline is the background risk of the population: a different country, a different decade, better treatment. That is why a model such as the Framingham equations can rank Canadians well and still over-predict their risk. The predictors describe the people; the baseline describes the setting.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: A calibration plot needs many riders
text:
A calibration plot needs many riders

5,000 simulated riders scored with Model A’s formula. Line: LOESS curve with 95% band. Circles: tenths of predicted risk. Ticks: where predictions fall. Dashed: perfect calibration.

TRIPOD+AI asks for a flexible calibration curve, such as LOESS, with summary measures, rather than grouped points alone. Simulated, not real. The true model has Model A’s slopes but an intercept of 0.5 instead of 2.0, so Model A over-predicts for everyone. Predictions only span about 0.74 to 0.96, because age, cane and superhero status are weak predictors: a short curve is honest. Recalibration moves the curve onto the diagonal.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Reading the plot, and how we recalibrated
text:
Reading the plot, and how we recalibrated

Calibration intercept: are predictions too high or too low overall? Ideal 0. Model A: −1.48, too high
Calibration slope: is the spread right? Ideal 1. Below 1, predictions are too extreme (common after overfitting). Model A: 0.95, about right
Only the intercept is wrong, so we shift every rider’s log-odds by the same amount:



fit <- glm(boarded ~ 1, offset = qlogis(model_a),
  family = binomial, data = sim)
sim$model_a_recal <- plogis(qlogis(sim$model_a) + coef(fit))


qlogis(): probability to log-odds; plogis(): back again. The offset keeps each rider’s log-odds fixed, so only the shift \(a\) = −1.48 is estimated. If the slope were off too, fit \(\text{logit}(p^{*}) = a + b\,\text{logit}(p)\) instead; machine learning calls this Platt scaling.

After recalibration the intercept is 0.00 and the slope still 0.95: shifting cannot change the spread. Here we recalibrated and checked on the same simulated riders, which flatters the result. In practice, recalibrate with data from the new setting, then check on fresh data.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: Summary measures: ICI, E50 and E90
text:
Summary measures: ICI, E50 and E90
How far is the curve from the diagonal, on average and at worst?
\[
\text{ICI} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left| p_i - \hat{y}_i \right|
\]
\(\hat{y}_i\): the LOESS curve’s observed proportion at rider \(i\)’s predicted probability. E50 and E90: the median and the 90th percentile of \(|p_i - \hat{y}_i|\).

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
A ladder of recalibration












Step
Method
What changes
Bus-stop problem




1
Intercept (in the large)
One shift
Model A over-predicts


1
Baseline (survival)
\(S_0(t)\)
The bus is late


2
Intercept and slope (Platt)
Shift and stretch
Model C is overconfident


3
Isotonic regression
Any increasing curve

4
Revision
Some coefficients
Model B’s superhero sign


5
Refit
Everything
Nothing else works






Climb only as far as you need: each step needs more data and can overfit the recalibration itself. Steps 1 to 3 keep the order of riders, so they cannot change discrimination; steps 4 and 5 change the model itself.

Start at the bottom. Calibration-in-the-large needs only the outcome rate in the new setting; the slope needs individual outcomes; isotonic regression needs many. Revision and refitting are no longer recalibration: they change the ranking, which is why Model B cannot be rescued by recalibration.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Step 2: intercept and slope
Model C was developed at a small, unusual bus stop. Same predictors, but the coefficients are too large: \(\text{logit}(p) = 1.5 + 0.25\,\tfrac{\text{age} - 60}{10} + 2.5\,\text{cane} − 2.5\,\text{superhero}\)
\[
\text{logit}(p^{*}) = a + b\,\text{logit}(p) \qquad a = −0.04, \quad b = 0.38
\]
\(b = 1\) is intercept-only recalibration (step 1). \(b < 1\): predictions are too extreme, so they are pulled toward the middle. \(b > 1\): too timid, so they are spread out. Machine learning calls this Platt scaling.


fit <- glm(boarded ~ qlogis(model_c), family = binomial, data = sim)
sim$model_c_recal <- predict(fit, type = "response")

Clara: \(\text{logit}(0.99) = 4.62\), so \(p^{*} = \text{plogis}(−0.04 + 0.38 \times 4.62) = 0.85\)
Every prediction moves toward the middle; the order of riders does not change.

Model C is sure Clara will board (0.99) and sure Batman will not. Shrinking the log-odds by b = 0.38 keeps the order but tempers the confidence. Five riders are far too few to estimate a slope; a and b come from the 5,000 simulated riders.

title: Calibration and discrimination
section: When the slope is wrong too
text:
When the slope is wrong too

Intercept-only recalibration moves the curve but leaves it tilted. Adding the slope straightens it. Isotonic regression fits any increasing curve, and checked on the riders it was fitted to, it flatters itself.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Beyond the formula

Isotonic regression: the best increasing staircase through the data. No formula, so it needs many riders, and it can overfit
Model revision: re-estimate the coefficients that are wrong. Model B’s superhero coefficient (2.5) points the wrong way; no shift or stretch can put Batman back in line
Refit: build a new model
Which step? Start at the bottom and climb only while the step below leaves miscalibration; check the result on fresh data


This is the logic of a closed testing procedure for choosing how far to update a model (Vergouwe and colleagues, Statistics in Medicine, 2017; doi:10.1002/sim.7179). Isotonic regression and Platt scaling are the methods most used in machine learning; logistic recalibration and baseline updating are the most used in clinical prediction.

Same ideas, two names. Students reading machine-learning papers and clinical prediction papers will meet both. Log loss, like the Brier score, mixes discrimination and calibration.

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Take-home points

Discrimination is about order: the c statistic counts correctly ranked pairs, which equals the area under the ROC curve
Calibration is about agreement: compare predicted with observed, on average (O/E) and across the range (calibration plot, ICI)
The Brier score, F1 and accuracy blend both, so they cannot tell you which problem a model has
Recalibration can fix calibration but never discrimination: start with the intercept, and add the slope only if needed
Time matters for calibration, not discrimination: a late bus breaks calibration and leaves the ranking alone

title: Calibration and discrimination
text:
Try it yourself


riders <- data.frame(
  rider     = c("Agnes", "Beatrice", "Clara", "Dorothy", "Batman"),
  age       = c(35, 80, 85, 80, 40),
  cane      = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0),
  superhero = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1),
  boarded   = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0)
)
# Model A (see the slide "Two models")
riders$model_a <- with(riders, plogis(
  2.0 + 0.1 * (age - 60) / 10 + 1.0 * cane - 1.0 * superhero
))
p <- riders$model_a

# c statistic (ties count half)
pairs <- expand.grid(
  boarded = which(riders$boarded == 1),
  waited = which(riders$boarded == 0)
)
better <- p[pairs$boarded] > p[pairs$waited]
tied <- p[pairs$boarded] == p[pairs$waited]
mean(better + 0.5 * tied)

mean(riders$boarded) / mean(p) # O/E
mean((p - riders$boarded)^2)   # Brier score

# Recalibrate: shift the log-odds
fit <- glm(boarded ~ 1, offset = qlogis(model_a), family = binomial, data = riders)
plogis(qlogis(p) + coef(fit))
